name: Berry Pink
lede: Berry Pink is a deep pink-purple from Ridgway's 1912 plates, and its name has nothing to do with the old pigment called pink, which was yellow.

sections.title: Two meanings of pink
sections.body:
In the color library Berry Pink comes from Ridgway's 1912 plates and the ISCC-NBS system, with Reddish Mulberry and Rosolane Purple listed as other names [1]. The books we hold say nothing about the origin of the name, so it is undocumented [1].

Older uses of berry and pink can mislead. The Pigment Compendium explains that the artists' pigment called pink was a yellow lake made from unripe buckthorn berries, sold as French berries or Avignon berries [2]. The word survived in names such as Dutch pink and English pink before it fell out of use [2]. That yellow is a different story from this swatch, which is a strong red-pink near [[raspberry]], [[cerise]] and [[rose-pink]] [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: In our archive of 23,781 paintings, a color within six units of this one covers at least five per cent of the canvas in only three, led by a 1900 Indian figure painting at about 29 per cent and Patrick Henry Bruce's Peinture/Nature Morte (1924) [3]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, so a match is not a pigment test [3].
